title: Does the FDA Protect Americans?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the history and role of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), from its roots under Abraham Lincoln's administration and chemist Charles Wetherill through the 1906 Food and Drugs Act (Wiley Act), the Poison Squad experiments led by Harvey Wiley, and the Upton Sinclair's The Jungle controversy. They cover the agency's organization and funding, including controversial prescription drug user fees, the 1982 Tylenol cyanide murders and tamper-resistant packaging, the thalidomide case and Frances Oldham Kelsey, the 1962 Kefauver-Harris amendments, antibiotics in livestock, GMO labeling, Vioxx, and the Zohydra painkiller, plus critiques from a Harvard/Hobby-style study on drug effectiveness and a Yale study on FDA approval standards.

entities.name: Department of Health and Human Services

segments.title: Opening banter and FDA setup
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners, joke about past herbal supplement episodes, and introduce the FDA as a controversial consumer protection agency that must balance speed of approval against safety.

segments.title: Pre-FDA origins and the 1906 Food and Drugs Act
segments.summary: Lincoln-era chemist Charles Wetherill was tasked with analyzing agricultural materials. Harvey Wiley and Peter Collier pushed for regulation over about 25 years. Upton Sinclair's The Jungle exposed meatpacking abuses, leading Congress to pass the Food and Drugs Act (Wiley Act) on June 30, 1906, which banned interstate trade in mislabeled and contaminated food, beverages, and medicines.

segments.title: The Poison Squad
segments.summary: Wiley set up the Poison Squad, volunteers who ate food laced with preservatives and additives such as borax, formaldehyde, and copper sulfate in a basement kitchen at FDA headquarters. Their testing showed these additives were harmful and public pressure helped lead to the Food and Drugs Act.

segments.title: FDA evolution and organization
segments.summary: The agency went through name changes and moved between departments, eventually landing under Health and Human Services in the late 1970s. Its organization includes the Commissioner's office, supporting organizations, five deputy commissioners, field offices, and a headquarters in Silver Spring, Maryland.

segments.title: Quiz on what the FDA regulates
segments.summary: Hosts run a true-or-false quiz on FDA jurisdiction, covering X-ray machines, pesticides (USDA), illicit drugs, donated blood, tobacco, poultry (USDA), and dairy. They note unregulated supplements and vague labeling terms like natural and light beer.

segments.title: 1982 Tylenol cyanide murders and tamper-resistant packaging
segments.summary: Cyanide-laced Extra Strength Tylenol in the Chicago area killed several people, including a twelve-year-old girl and members of one family. The killer was never identified. Johnson & Johnson issued a national alert and led the push for tamper-resistant packaging, and Congress made tampering with medicine a federal crime. The FDA later made tamper-resistant packaging mandatory about six years later.

segments.title: FDA scope, inspections, staffing, and international reach
segments.summary: The FDA regulates roughly 20 cents of every consumer dollar, about one trillion dollars in goods and services, and conducts about 16,000 facility inspections per year. With fewer than 15,000 total employees, it has an office in Beijing and oversees imported products sold in America.

segments.title: FDA funding and user fees
segments.summary: The FDA is funded about $4.4 billion, roughly $2.6 billion from the Treasury and close to $2 billion from user fees. The Prescription Drug User Fee Act lets drug companies pay fees for faster review, raising concerns about industry influence. Critics such as Raymond Woosley argue protection should come before serving industry, and a Yale study criticized inconsistent approval standards, while a Forbes response defended flexibility for rare diseases.

segments.title: Drug effectiveness study, Vioxx, and historical successes and failures
segments.summary: A Harvard-linked paper in the Journal of Law, Medicine and Ethics argued that most new drugs are no more effective than existing ones, and that many cause serious harm. Hosts also discuss antibiotics in livestock, the FDA's position on antibiotic resistance, GMO labeling petitions, and Vioxx, which stayed on the market for four more years after a 2000 study showed heart attack risk until Merck withdrew it. They discuss thalidomide, where Frances Oldham Kelsey blocked approval in the US, and the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments.

segments.title: Zohydra and opioid abuse
segments.summary: Zohydra, a pure hydrocodone painkiller approved by the FDA, lacked tamper resistance, prompting concern about abuse. Hosts link oxycodone abuse, tamper-resistant reformulation, and the heroin epidemic, and note that hydrocodone opioid deaths rose fourfold between roughly 2000 and 2010.

segments.title: Listener mail from author Gina Domico
segments.summary: A young adult dark-humor author says the show inspired elements of her books and named high school characters after the hosts. Show gives contact and website information.
